item.title: "When the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the…
item.description:
"When the eye sees a form, the monk does not grasp the general feature, does not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — that cause the monk restrains, guards the eye faculty... By means of this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences an internal feeling of ease, unblemished."

From: Dīgha Nikāya 2 – Sāmaññaphalasutta

item.title: “Just as, monks, this body subsists in dependence on food, with food as condition it stands; without food it does not stand. So too, monks,…
item.description:
“Just as, monks, this body subsists in dependence on food, with food as condition it stands; without food it does not stand. So too, monks, the five hindrances subsist in dependence on food, with food as condition they stand; without food they do not stand. And what, monks, is the food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire? There is, monks, the sign of the beautiful. Frequent unwise attention to it — this is the food for the arising of unarisen sensual desire, and for the growth and increase of arisen sensual desire.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 46.2
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, not knowing and not seeing the eye as it actually is; not knowing and not seeing forms … eye-consciousness … eye-contact as it actually…
item.description:
“Monks, not knowing and not seeing the eye as it actually is; not knowing and not seeing forms … eye-consciousness … eye-contact as it actually is; not knowing and not seeing the feeling—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—that arises dependent on eye-contact as it actually is, then he becomes attached to the eye, to forms, to eye-consciousness, to eye-contact. Dependent on eye-contact, the feeling—pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—arises; he becomes attached to that feeling. When he dwells contemplating gratification, attached, tied, infatuated, the five aggregates of clinging accumulate for the future. And his craving—which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there—increases. His bodily torments increase, his mental torments increase, his bodily fevers increase, his mental fevers increase, his bodily pains increase, his mental pains increase. He experiences bodily suffering and mental suffering.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 149 – Mahāsaḷāyatanikasutta

item.title: Then the Blessed One, knowing “This is Māra the Evil One,” recited this verse to Māra: Forms, sounds, tastes, and smells, And all contacts, all…
item.description:
Then the Blessed One, knowing “This is Māra the Evil One,” recited this verse to Māra:
Forms, sounds, tastes, and smells,
And all contacts, all phenomena —
These are terrifying things,
Bewildering beings in the world.
A disciple of the Perfectly Enlightened One,
Mindful, transcends them all,
Transcending Māra’s power,
Shining like the sun.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.17
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, these five perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, ending in the deathless. What five? The…
item.description:
“Monks, these five perceptions, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, ending in the deathless. What five? The perception of impermanence, the perception of not-self, the perception of death, the perception of disgust with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world. These five perceptions, monks, when developed and cultivated, are of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, ending in the deathless.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.62

item.title: “Monks, a monk who thinks: ‘Covetousness, unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons the covetousness, unrighteous greed that is a…
item.description:
“Monks, a monk who thinks: ‘Covetousness, unrighteous greed is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons the covetousness, unrighteous greed that is a defilement of the mind; thinks: ‘Ill-will is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons ill-will, the defilement of the mind; anger … hostility … hypocrisy … spite … envy … stinginess … deceit … fraud … obstinacy … impetuosity … conceit … arrogance … vanity; thinks: ‘Heedlessness is a defilement of the mind’ and, knowing that, abandons heedlessness, the defilement of the mind.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 7 – Vatthūpamasutta

item.title: “Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. This, monks, is not called the ocean…
item.description:
“Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. This, monks, is not called the ocean in the noble one’s discipline. Here, this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, with its ascetics and brahmins, with its gods and humans, for the most part is submerged in them, tangled like a ball of thread, covered like a tangled skein, become like a tangled grass rope, unable to pass beyond the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower realm, saṃsāra. Monks, there are sounds … odors … tastes … touches … Monks, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. This, monks, is not called the ocean in the noble one’s discipline. Here, this world … for the most part is submerged in them … unable to pass beyond the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower realm, saṃsāra.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.229

item.title: When feeling a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not to be clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not to…
item.description:
When feeling a pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not to be clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not to be delighted in.’ When feeling a painful feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not to be clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not to be delighted in.’ When feeling a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he understands: ‘It is impermanent’; he understands: ‘It is not to be clung to’; he understands: ‘It is not to be delighted in.’ If he feels a pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is not bound. If he feels a painful feeling … If he feels a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, he feels it as one who is not bound. When he feels a feeling ending with the body, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling ending with the body.’ When he feels a feeling ending with life, he understands: ‘I feel a feeling ending with life.’ He understands: ‘With the breakup of the body, after death, everything that is felt, in which he no longer delights, will become cool right here.’ Just as, Assaji, an oil lamp burns in dependence on oil and a wick. When the oil and wick of that lamp are exhausted, with no further fuel, the lamp is extinguished. So too, Assaji, a monk, when feeling a feeling ending with the body, understands … when feeling a feeling ending with life, understands … after death, everything that is felt, in which he no longer delights, becomes cool.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.88
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Kulla: Kulla went to the charnel ground, Saw a woman abandoned, Thrown away in the cemetery, Food for worms. “Kulla, look at this body…
item.description:
Elder Kulla:

Kulla went to the charnel ground,
Saw a woman abandoned,
Thrown away in the cemetery,
Food for worms.

“Kulla, look at this body —
Diseased, foul, stinking,
Oozing, seeping,
Delighting fools.”

Having taken up the mirror of Dhamma,
I attained right view.
I contemplated this body —
Empty inside and out.

As it is below, so above,
As above, so below,
As below, so above,
As above, so below.

As by day, so by night,
As by night, so by day,
As before, so after,
As after, so before.

Such a one does not delight
In the five kinds of music.
When one-pointed,
Rightly meditating on the Dhamma.

From: Theragāthā 6.4
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And how, monks, is dwelling heedfully? If one lives with restraint of the eye faculty, monks, his mind is not defiled by forms cognizable by…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is dwelling heedfully? If one lives with restraint of the eye faculty, monks, his mind is not defiled by forms cognizable by the eye. For one with an undefiled mind, gladness arises. With gladness, rapture arises. With rapture, the body becomes tranquil. With a tranquil body, he experiences ease. For one at ease, the mind becomes concentrated. When the mind is concentrated, phenomena are clearly seen. When phenomena are clearly seen, he is called ‘one who dwells heedfully’ … the ear faculty … the nose faculty … the tongue faculty … the body faculty … If one lives with restraint of the mind faculty, his mind is not defiled by phenomena cognizable by the mind. For one with an undefiled mind, gladness arises … he is called ‘one who dwells heedfully.’ Thus, monks, is dwelling heedfully.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.97
